q: Vintage, variety and origin claims on an Australian label are checked by auditing a winery's own paperwork rather than by judging the wine in the glass. What is that audit scheme called?
exp: The Label Integrity Program follows fruit from the weighbridge to the bottle, so a false claim is caught in the records rather than by a panel. The Geographical Indications Committee is a real body doing a different job: it determines boundaries, it does not police labels.

q: Dense, dark and soft-edged at fifteen percent alcohol, chocolate and ripe plum with a warm sweet finish, grown on a warm valley floor an hour north-east of Adelaide. Which region and grape?
exp: The Barossa floor is warm, dry and low-lying, so sugar accumulates fast and acidity falls away, giving weight and sweetness of fruit rather than tension. It is the style that made Australian red wine famous abroad and it remains the country's benchmark for the grape.

q: Climb east out of the Barossa floor into hills a few hundred metres higher, and the calling card changes from a broad red to a dry white of lime and chalky grip. Which region have you reached?
exp: Eden Valley shares the Barossa zone with the valley floor but sits higher, cooler and on ancient weathered granite, and Riesling rather than Shiraz is what it is known for. Two neighbouring regions inside one zone produce wines with almost nothing in common.

q: Lutheran families from Silesia and Prussia settled one Australian valley from 1842, and their village names, bakeries and smokehouses are still in place. Which valley did they plant?
exp: German-speaking settlers gave the Barossa its Bethany, its Langmeil and its Krondorf, and they put vines in beside the wheat. Six generations of unbroken farming on the same blocks is why so much of that original planting material is still in the ground.

q: Old Shiraz in the Barossa often stands as a low free-standing shrub, with no wire, no post and no trellis anywhere near it. What is that training form called?
opts: Bush vine, also known as head training
exp: A head-trained bush vine carries its own canopy without any support, and its own leaves shade the fruit from a fierce sun. It suits a dry-grown, low-yielding old block and is far too labour-intensive for anything planted with a machine harvester in mind.

q: Alongside Shiraz, two other heat-tolerant varieties came to the Barossa in the nineteenth century and are now blended with it under a three-letter shorthand. Which two?
exp: GSM stands for Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro, the last being the Australian name for Mourvedre. All three tolerate heat and drought, which is why the same trio recurs across the southern Rhone and Spain's Mediterranean coast.

q: Vanilla, coconut and sweet baking spice sit over the fruit of a traditional Barossa Shiraz, and none of it comes from the grape. Where does it come from?
opts: American oak, whose lactones give exactly those aromas
Grape concentrate added shortly before bottling
An extended period on lees before bottling
French oak, which is the standard cooperage for the style
exp: American oak is far richer than French in the lactone that reads as coconut and vanilla, and it was cheap and available when the style was formed. French oak gives finer, more savoury spice instead, so the choice between them changes the wine as much as the vineyard does.

q: The Barossa keeps a register that ranks a vineyard purely by its age, with rungs at thirty-five, seventy, one hundred and one hundred and twenty-five years. What is the top rung called?
exp: The Old Vine Charter runs Old Vine, Survivor Vine, Centenarian Vine and Ancestor Vine, the last requiring at least a hundred and twenty-five years of production. It exists because a vineyard that old has no legal protection of any kind and is worth more documented than pulled.

q: Bone dry, around twelve percent, lime juice and a hard chalky finish that turns to toast after a decade in bottle: this white is the making of a set of narrow north-south valleys well north of Adelaide. Name the region and the grape.
exp: Clare Riesling is fermented dry and bottled without any oak, so nothing stands between the fruit and the acid. With age it turns toasty and takes on a lime-marmalade depth, and the screwcap it has worn since 2000 is largely why that ageing is now dependable.

q: Clare's summers are hot and it lies well inland, away from any moderating sea, yet its Riesling keeps a ferocious acidity. What preserves it?
opts: Afternoon sea breezes arriving off the Southern Ocean
A limestone subsoil that adds acidity to the juice
Height, and the cold nights that come with it
Constant cloud cover through the summer months
exp: The Clare valleys sit several hundred metres up, and on a clear night at that height the temperature falls sharply. Respiration burns acid through a warm night and stalls through a cold one, so the wide daily swing is what leaves the wine its bite.

q: Thirty-five kilometres south of Adelaide the vineyards run down toward a gulf, and a sea breeze arrives most summer afternoons to take the heat out of ripening. Which region?
exp: McLaren Vale lies between the Mount Lofty Ranges and Gulf St Vincent, and the water is close enough to change the afternoon. The climate reads as Mediterranean, which is why Shiraz, Grenache and a lengthening list of Italian and Spanish varieties all succeed there.

q: Deep sand at Blewitt Springs, old unirrigated bush vines and a retreat from heavy extraction have made one southern Rhone variety a McLaren Vale speciality, pale and perfumed rather than dense. Which?
exp: Grenache ripens late and to high sugar, so for decades it was picked overripe and either buried in oak or fortified. Picked earlier off old sandy blocks it gives a translucent, red-fruited wine with fine tannin, and that reversal is among the clearest style changes in modern Australian wine.

q: Immediately east of Adelaide the land climbs into ranges where Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay hold a nervy acidity the plains below cannot manage. Which region?
exp: The Adelaide Hills run along the Mount Lofty Ranges and much of the vineyard sits above four hundred metres. It is one of South Australia's coolest regions and supplies both crisp still whites and base wine for sparkling.

q: Two named subregions inside the Adelaide Hills appear on labels for cool-climate Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Which pair?
exp: Lenswood and Piccadilly Valley are the only two subregions the Adelaide Hills has registered, and both sit high and cold enough for a long slow ripening. Watervale and Polish Hill River belong to Clare, and Blewitt Springs and Seaview to McLaren Vale.

q: A narrow cigar-shaped strip of red-brown topsoil lies over soft white limestone with the water table close beneath, and it grows Australia's most celebrated Cabernet. What is that topsoil called?
exp: Terra rossa is a thin iron-rich clay left behind as the limestone below it weathered, and the strip carrying it is only a couple of kilometres wide. Roots pass through it into the limestone, which drains freely yet keeps water within reach, so the vine is neither drowned nor starved.

q: Cassis, mint and a firm dry structure, from a flat cool strip in the far south-east of South Australia close to the Victorian border. Which variety carries that reputation?
exp: Coonawarra ripens Cabernet slowly enough to shed the green pyrazine edge without surrendering acid or structure, which very few warm countries manage. The eucalypt or mint note is a regional signature rather than a fault.
